seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: Many thanks for the suit which Mr Eliot brought. It fits quite well except for the shoulders which are rather tight. I shall be glad of it in the winter as it seems to be wool. I hate the cold. I had not much opportunity of speaking with Mr Eliot and Mr Lewis, whose arrival surprised me, but managed to catch a few of their phrases in the lulls of l’ami Fritz’s volubility. A good thing is that he usually laughs next day over all the noise he made the night before. E abbastanza simpatico questo .

Miss Serruys and Miss Barney spoke to Lugne Poe who will speak to them this week. I wrote to Mr Bradley (re Exiles & Portrait ) who wrote to Miss Serruys who wrote to me who wrote to Mrs Bloch to write to Benda who visited me who wrote to Davray who wrote to me that he had written to
Valette Vallette
who so far hasn’t written to anybody.

I send back the prospectus you sent me. Among the papers you left with me are undelivered letters for Mr Dujardin and Mr A. Lichtenberger (without his address). What, if anything, is to be done with these?

Who has the dossier I sent you? Mr Aldington? If so, I should be glad to have it returned to me at his convenience. And, if you see Mr Rodker , will you please ask him to let me have a copy of the Little Review as soon as he receives a new number.

Two chapters of the novel are translated. The translator appears to find the work very difficult. She told me that Mr Aldington proposed to her to translate some book by Miss Sinclair or Miss Richardson. I forget which. Translate in haste and repent at leisure. The Swedish translator sends me lists of difficulties by every second post. The Spaniard , till now, has not written. He (or more probably, she) is, I expect, spinning a yarn all of his own.

postscript.p:
P.S. A bad day for me. Francis Joseph’s birthday. The anniversary of my seizure in the Bahnhofstrasse, Zurich, with subsequent violent glaucoma.
Via, presto
.

div.note: The American poet and critic T.S. Eliot (1888-1965) visited Paris on 15-16 August and dined there with JJ and the English writer and artist Wyndham Lewis (1882-1957). Eliot brought with him a parcel, entrusted to him by Pound, that contained a gift for JJ of some used clothing and a pair of old brown shoes (see JJ to Pound, 13 August 1920, notes). Eliot described JJ shortly after the meeting as “a quiet but rather dogmatic man [with] a sense of his own importance. He has a sort of gravity which seems more Protestant than Catholic” (The Letters of T.S. Eliot, vol. 1, ed. Valerie Eliot [New York: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1988], 402-03).

Fritz-René Vanderpyl (1876-1965), Belgian (often described as Dutch) novelist, poet, gastronome, and art critic for Le Petit Parisien. He was listed among pledged contributors to the New York magazine The Dial, of which Pound was a paid agent and correspondent at this time. Pound admired Vanderpyl and considered him an “amusin’ cuss” (The Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 1915-1924, ed. Timothy Materer [Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1991], 192). Urged by Pound, JJ made Vanderpyl’s acquaintance in Paris in July 1920 and received from him an inscribed copy of his book, Mon chant de guerre (Paris, 1917), which John Rodker found to be “a very restrained war-song – being in simple rhythm, felicitous phrasing and a not too original out-look. Occasionally he interposes English verses of an amazing triteness and one wonders why this sort of thing sounds so much more possible in French. … The book is worth reading because it feels ‘sound’” (“Books,” The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 5 [September 1918]: 48). Vanderpyl contributed to various magazines in this period, including Poetry, and published an appreciation of the French artist Maurice Vlaminck, with reproductions of his paintings, in The Dial, vol. 69, no. 6 (December 1920): 590-91. In “The Island of Paris: A Letter,” The Dial, vol. 69, no. 5 (November 1920): 515-18, Pound described Vanderpyl as one of the “fine human objects … perched reading on his balcony, his head like a round dreaming cannon-ball atop the stubby structure of his person.” Eliot made a drawing of JJ, Wyndham Lewis, Vanderpyl, and himself, attended by a perplexed Parisian waiter, with Vanderpyl gesticulating and carrying on with what JJ in this letter calls “volubility” (The Letters of T.S. Eliot, 403).
It. “This is rather likable.” Or more colloquially, “I rather like this in him.”

Newly arrived in Paris and wanting to enhance his calling card, JJ was eager to have his play Exiles and his novel A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man translated into French. Jenny Serruys (1886-1983), a French literary figure, was an early candidate for translating A Portrait, but she did not do so. (Ludmila Bloch-Savitsky [1881-1957], another new acquaintance of JJ’s, published a French translation of A Portrait in 1924.) Much later, Serruys did produce a French translation of Exiles (Les Exilés) which was published under her married name J.S. Bradley by nrf Gallimard in Paris in 1950. (For more on Serruys and Bloch-Savitsky, see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes.)

Natalie Clifford Barney (1876-1972), expatriate American playwright, poet, and novelist, was famous for her Latin Quarter salon and, in the garden of her pavilion, her classical Temple of Friendship, where writers and artists of all stripes and nationalities met and conversed. Pound, who was a good friend of Barney’s, facilitated JJ’s contact with her early on in his Paris stay. At one of her soirées, attended by Paul Valéry and other writers, JJ found himself “ill at ease, averse as always to discoursing at large, but he made some effort to converse with them about French literature, and had got as far as saying he couldn’t bear Racine and Corneille when Miss Barney, embarrassed by this opinion, interrupted rudely, ‘Don’t you think that sort of remark shows something about the person who says it?’ Joyce was silent, and spent the rest of the evening draped around a column in the drawing room” (Ellmann, JJ 488).

Aurélien-Marie Lugné (1869-1940), known as Lugné-Poë, was a French actor, theater director, and scenic designer who at Paris’s Théâtre de l’Œuvre and other venues produced the drama of Henrik Ibsen, Gerhart Hauptmann, August Strindberg, and other playwrights. Jenny Serruys and Natalie Clifford Barney (see notes 4 and 5 above) were enlisted to help persuade Lugné-Poë to produce Exiles, and JJ uncharacteristically agreed to allow the play to be adapted. After some indecision, Lugné-Poë told JJ that he would stage it in December 1920 or January 1921, but in June 1921 he concluded that a production of Exiles would lose money (Ellmann, JJ 497-98). JJ told Harriet Shaw Weaver that Lugné-Poë had written him “a most insolent letter in slang to say that he was not such a fool as to put on the piece and lose 15,000 francs. My consolation is that I win a box of preserved apricots – a bet I made with Mr Pound (who was optimistic) after a cursory inspection of the director aforesaid” (LI 166). An adaptation of Jenny Serruys Bradley’s translation of Exiles was finally performed at the Théâtre Gramont, Paris, in 1956, directed by Hélène Gerber. Sylvia Beach wrote that this French premiere “was so well done I regretted that Joyce was no longer there to see it” (Shakespeare and Company [1959; rpt. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 1991], 167).

William Aspenwall Bradley (1878-1939) was an American writer and critic and the fiancé of Jenny Serruys. Together, they assisted JJ in various ways during his first months in Paris (see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes).

The Russian-born Ludmila Bloch-Savitsky (1881-1957) was married to a railroad chief engineer, Marcel Bloch (1881-1951). They offered JJ a flat, rent-free, for his first three months in Paris. Bloch-Savitsky published her French translation of JJ’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man in 1924 (see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes).

Julien Benda (1867-1956), French novelist, philosopher, and cultural critic, whom JJ met during his first weeks in Paris (Ellmann, JJ 489). As a result of Pound’s efforts, Benda’s critique Belphégor: essai sur l'esthétique de la présente société française was serialized in English translation in The Dial. In it, Benda announced the general thesis: “Modern French society requires of works of art that they make it experience emotions and sensations and no longer expects to realize from works of art any kind of intellectual pleasure” (vol. 69, no.3 [September 1920], 252). Benda’s anti-Bergsonism and his elevation of clear, distinct ideas above popular doctrines of time, emotion, and flux appealed to Pound, who in 1920 considered him the “best mind” he had encountered in Paris (Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 191). In 1927, Benda published La Trahison des Clercs, which argued that modern European intellectuals had abdicated dispassionate reason in political matters and had contributed to nationalism and warmongering. The work was translated into English by Richard Aldington as The Great Betrayal (1928).

note.p: JJ was hoping that a French translation of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man would be published serially in the journal Mercure de France, which was founded and edited by Alfred Vallette (1858-1935), and for which the French critic Henry Davray (1873-1944) wrote often as a specialist in English literature. JJ wrote Davray on 11 August 1920 that he hoped the Mercure would “arbitrer l’artiste irlandais, jeune homme” (“shelter the Irish artist as a young man”) (LIII 14-15). But on 20 October 1920, JJ reported to Jenny Serruys that the Mercure had given “aucune signe de vie” (“no sign of life”) (LIII 25). Other French journals declined it as well. The French translation of A Portrait had to await publication, as a book, in 1924 by Ludmila Savitsky. Davray had previously published a favorable account of JJ’s Exiles and other writings in “Lettres anglaises,” Mercure de France, vol. 121, no. 495 (1 February 1919 ): 512-18.

The paragraph of the present letter beginning “Miss Serruys” echoes the rhythms of the passage in the “Cyclops” episode of Ulysses that ridicules Leopold Bloom’s praise of “love” as the true essence of “life”: “His Majesty the King loves Her Majesty the Queen. Mrs Norman W. Tupper loves officer Taylor. You love a certain person. And this person loves that other person because everybody loves somebody but God loves everybody” (U 12.1498-1501).

div.note: It is uncertain what “prospectus” Pound had sent JJ, but around this time he was mailing circulars for John Rodker’s Ovid Press (see Ezra Pound to His Parents: Letters 1895-1929, ed. Mary de Rachewiltz et al. [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010], 469). The short-lived Ovid Press, an artisanal hand press and publishing firm in London, issued, among other modernist writings, a limited first edition of Pound’s Hugh Selwyn Mauberley in June 1920. Rodker had hoped to be the initial publisher of Ulysses in some book format, but this plan did not come to fruition (for a fuller account, see JJ to Pound, letter fragment, late July 1920, notes).

Édouard Dujardin (1861-1949) was a French author and pioneer of the stream-of-consciousness literary technique, especially in his 1888 novel, Les Lauriers sont coupés, which has been credited with influencing JJ’s use of interior monologue in Ulysses. JJ publicly praised Dujardin and wanted to see his work more widely recognized. Dujardin and JJ inscribed and dedicated books to each other. JJ inscribed a copy of Ulysses to “E.D. Annunciator of the interior monologue, the impenitent thief. JJ.,” though he wrote privately to Harriet Shaw Weaver that in exchanging inscriptions, he felt he had given Dujardin “cake for bread” (LI 287). JJ later helped Stuart Gilbert with his English translation of Les Lauriers sont coupés, which was titled We’ll to the Woods No More (for JJ, Dujardin, and the English translation, see Ellmann, JJ 519-20 & n.*, 665). During 1920, as paid agent and foreign correspondent of The Dial, Pound was actively canvassing French authors for submissions to that New York magazine. It is likely that JJ discussed Dujardin with Pound when the two met in Sirmione in June 1920 or in Paris in July.

Probably André Lichtenberger (1870-1940), French novelist, sociologist, and historian. His recent books included a novel, Le Sang Nouveau (1914). It is likely that he was among the numerous French writers that Pound was contacting in his role as agent and foreign correspondent for the New York magazine The Dial.

note.p: The “dossier” JJ refers to was a collection of papers documenting his 1918-1919 legal dispute in Zurich with Henry Carr and the subsequent conspiracy of British consular officials that JJ believed had formed to undermine him and the English Players, the acting troupe that he had cofounded and managed in Zurich. JJ wrote a statement, dated 28 April 1919, setting forth the history of perceived outrages (LII 438-40). Pound, who received JJ’s dossier around the same time, complained to JJ that “you have given me no ‘case’ to present,” only “a lot of documents proving that a company of players put on a Chesterton play (for which they ought all to be poisoned until dead of gangrene)” (Pound/Joyce 153-54). Pound said that he would “leave things in [Richard Aldington’s] charge” (ibid., 154). The English writer and critic Richard Aldington (1892-1962) became a sort of official holder of the dossier (LII 442). In July 1927, JJ was still trying to get “the dossier of the English Players” back from Aldington (LIII 161-62). (For a fuller account of the Zurich litigation and the Rumbold affair, see JJ to Pound, 1 April 1919, notes.)

Pound had known Aldington since 1911 and had included him, along with JJ, H.D. (Hilda Doolittle, 1886-1961), and other poets, in the groundbreaking anthology, Des Imagistes (1914). Aldington had been assistant editor of the English magazine The Egoist when it serialized A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1914-1915). He and T.S. Eliot later informally agreed to write competing reviews of Ulysses in progress. Aldington published “The Influence of Mr. James Joyce” in the English Review (London), vol. 32 (April 1921): 333-41, praising Ulysses as “remarkable” and “an astonishing psychological document,” but worrying that its bold experiments in style would, among its imitators, degenerate into “incoherence, affectation, and wordy confusion,” since JJ with his “great undisciplined talent” was “more dangerous than a ship-load of Dadaistes” (333, 339). He also wrote: “Ulysses is more bitter, more sordid, more ferociously satirical than anything Mr. Joyce has yet written. It is a tremendous libel on humanity which I at least am not clever enough to refute” (336). Eliot took more than two years to reply to Aldington. Armed with the completed Ulysses and the Homeric parallels that JJ had circulated among the faithful, Eliot retorted that, while he did not know if it was “possible to libel humanity,” JJ had employed Homeric myth as “a continuous parallel between contemporaneity and antiquity … a method which others must pursue after him.” So much for Aldington’s dread of JJ’s undisciplined influence. Eliot added that JJ’s method was “simply a way of controlling, of ordering, of giving a shape and a significance to the immense panorama of futility and anarchy which is contemporary history” (“Ulysses, Order, and Myth,” The Dial, vol. 75, no. 5 [November 1923]: 481, 483).

div.note: The English writer, poet, and publisher John Rodker (1894-1955) had become foreign editor of The Little Review after Pound’s departure from that New York magazine. For a fuller account of Rodker’s role in JJ’s life and work at this time, see JJ to Pound, letter fragment, late July 1920, notes.

Ludmila Bloch-Savitsky struggled to translate faithfully and sensitively JJ’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. She complained that JJ was “not involved enough in a translation process that he did not take seriously,” and he blamed her “for delaying the translation he needed quickly to launch his career in France” (Leonid Livak, “‘A Thankless Occupation’: James Joyce and His Translator Ludmila Savitzky,” Joyce Studies Annual [2013]: 39). Although the bulk of the translation was completed by April 1921, its publication was delayed for various reasons and appeared in 1924 as Dedalus; Portrait de l’artiste jeune par lui-même, with Éditions de la Sirène of Paris.

The French poet and critic André Spire (1868–1966) had “arranged for Savitzky’s collaboration as a literary critic in British and American journals and encouraged her first translations from the works of Richard Aldington, Hilda Doolittle, F.S. Flint, and May Sinclair, a list she expanded to Ezra Pound, John Rodker, Virginia Woolf, and to Joyce himself” (Livak, “‘A Thankless Occupation,’” 35). May Sinclair (1863-1946) was a British writer who published novels, short stories, and poetry, was an active suffragist, and wrote critical assessments of modernist poetry and prose. She may have been the first to use the phrase “stream of consciousness” to describe modernist narrative technique in her review of part of the novel sequence Pilgrimage by the British author Dorothy Richardson (1873-1957) (May Sinclair, “The Novels of Dorothy Richardson,” The Egoist, vol. 5, no. 4 [April 1918]: 57-59; see also Sydney Kaplan, “‘Featureless Freedom’ or Ironic Submission: Dorothy Richardson and May Sinclair,” College English, vol. 32, no. 8 [May 1971]: 914-17).

The Swedish translation by Ebba Atterbom (1868-1961) of A Portrait was published, under the title Ett porträtt av konstnären som ung, in Stockholm in 1921. JJ managed to work Atterbom into Finnegans Wake: “The Fin had a flux and his Ebba a ride. / Attabom, attabom, attabombomboom!” (FW 103).

The Spanish translation of A Portrait, by Alfonso Donado (pseudonym of Dámaso Alonso, 1898-1990), was published under the title El Artista Adolescente (Retrato) in 1926 in Madrid. JJ answered Alonso’s questions and referred him to the French translation of A Portrait for hints (LIII 128-30), but Alonso thought that his translation was “closer to the original character of the novel than the French one. There is in some respects a likeness between Spanish and Irish people’s idiosyncrasy” (LIII 129 n.1). T.S. Eliot found Alonso’s translation of A Portrait, with its introduction by Antonio Marichalar, interesting enough to merit review in The New Criterion, vol. 5, no. 1 (January 1927): 158.

JJ suffered a severe attack of lumbago followed by glaucoma in August 1917, prompting his ophthalmologist, Ernst Sidler, to perform an iridectomy on his right eye at the Zurich Augenklinik a few days later. Resulting exudation from the eye during convalescence permanently reduced JJ’s vision (Ellmann, JJ 417).
“Away, quickly,” as one might say of a bad omen or memory. The phrase is also found in several places in Mozart’s operas, such as the epilogue in Don Giovanni, where it means “Hurry up!”
